entry: Chemical stimulant and [[Alkaloid|alkaloid]] found primarily in plants of the nightshade family, notably [[Tobacco|tobacco]], and is also synthesized. Tobacco leaves contain about 0.6–3% nicotine by dry weight, with smaller traces in [[Tomato|tomatoes]], [[Potato|potatoes]] and [[Eggplant|eggplants]]. In humans nicotine acts mainly as a stimulant, activating nicotinic acetylcholine receptors and releasing [[Dopamine|dopamine]], which produces increased alertness, reduced anxiety and mild euphoria. Nicotine is highly addictive. An average [[Cigarette|cigarette]] yields about 2 mg of absorbed nicotine. Nicotine replacement products such as gums, patches and lozenges deliver it in slower, lower doses and are used to help people quit smoking; a 2018 Cochrane Collaboration review found that they raise the chances of quitting by 50–60%. Nicotine is not classified as a [[Carcinogen|carcinogen]] by the International Agency for Research on Cancer or the U.S. Surgeon General. At high doses it can cause poisoning and respiratory paralysis.

Danish theoretical physicist whose foundational work on atomic structure and quantum theory earned the 1922 Nobel Prize in Physics. He also worked as a philosopher and a promoter of scientific research. He developed the [[Bohr model]] of the [[Atom|atom]], in which electron energy levels are discrete and electrons revolve in stable orbits around the [[Atomic nucleus|atomic nucleus]]. The model has since been superseded, but its principles remain valid. He founded the Institute of Theoretical Physics at the [[University of Copenhagen]], which opened in 1920 and is now known as the Niels Bohr Institute. He helped refugees from [[Nazism]] during the 1930s. In 1943, facing arrest, he fled to Sweden and then Britain, where he joined the British Tube Alloys project and the British mission to the [[Manhattan Project]]. After the war he called for international cooperation on nuclear energy and was involved in establishing [[CERN]].

Norwegian mathematician who made pioneering contributions in several fields. His most famous result was the first complete proof of the impossibility of solving the general quintic equation in radicals, a problem that had been unresolved for over 250 years. He was also an innovator in the field of elliptic functions and the discoverer of Abelian functions. Most of his work was done in six or seven years of his working life, and he made his discoveries while living in poverty. He died of [[Tuberculosis|tuberculosis]]. The French mathematician [[Charles Hermite]] said: "Abel has left mathematicians enough to keep them busy for five hundred years." [[Adrien-Marie Legendre]] said: "What a head the young Norwegian has!"

British politician and broadcaster, leader of Reform UK. He was a member of the [[Conservative Party (UK)|Conservative Party]] from 1978 to 1992 and became a prominent Eurosceptic. He was elected to the [[European Parliament]] in 1999 and led the UK Independence Party from 2006 to 2009 and from 2010 to 2016. In 2018 he co-founded the Brexit Party, renamed Reform UK in 2021. He resigned as MP for Clacton in July 2026 while under investigation over undeclared gifts, and won the resulting by-election with 63.3% of the vote. He has hosted programs on GB News since 2021.

English food writer, television cook and former journalist known for a relaxed and indulgent approach to cooking. She has sold more than 12 million cookery books worldwide, including *How to Be a Domestic Goddess* (2000), which won the British Book Award for Author of the Year. After graduating from the [[University of Oxford]], she became deputy literary editor of *The Sunday Times* in 1986. Her UK television programmes include *Nigella Bites*. In 2026 she became a judge on the Channel 4 baking competition *The Great British Bake Off*.

Annual [[Flowering plant|flowering plant]] of the buttercup family, native to western Asia and eastern Europe. Its seeds are used as a spice in many cuisines, including the mixture *panch phoron* in Bengali cooking and some varieties of naan. The name *Nigella* is a diminutive of [[Latin|Latin]] *niger*, "black", referring to the colour of the seeds. Seeds have been found at ancient Egyptian sites, including the Tomb of Tutankhamun. The Persian physician [[Avicenna]] described it as a treatment for dyspnea. Oils make up 32% to 40% of the seed composition.

Proposed family of African languages spoken across most of [[Sub-Saharan Africa]], uniting the Mande languages with the Atlantic–Congo languages. If valid, it would be the world's largest language family by number of member languages, the third-largest by number of speakers and Africa's largest by area. Ethnologue lists 1,540 named languages. The family has around 600 million native speakers as of 2025, and the [[Bantu languages]] alone account for 350 million people (2015), half of the total. The most widely spoken language by total speakers is [[Swahili]], a [[Lingua franca|lingua franca]] in parts of eastern and southeastern Africa. The core Atlantic–Congo group is widely accepted, and its most distinctive feature is a noun-class system. The connection of the Mande languages is often contested. The family most likely originated in West or Central Africa, before the [[Bantu expansion]].

Main river of West Africa, about 4,180 kilometres (2,600 miles) long and the third-longest in Africa, after the [[Nile]] and the [[Congo River]]. Its drainage basin covers 2,117,700 km² (817,600 sq mi). The river rises in the Guinea Highlands near the Sierra Leone border and runs in a crescent through southwest [[Mali]], then along the border with [[Benin]] and through [[Nigeria]]. It discharges through the Niger Delta into the [[Gulf of Guinea]]. Its main tributary is the Benue River. Where its gradient suddenly decreases, the river forms the Inner Niger Delta, a region of braided streams, marshes and large lakes that is extremely productive for fishing and agriculture. The river carries only about a tenth as much sediment as the Nile and floods yearly, beginning in September, peaking in November and ending by May.

Landlocked country in West Africa, officially the Republic of the Niger, with a land area of almost 1.27 million km² and over 80% of its territory in the [[Sahara]]. It is the sixth-largest country in Africa and the second-largest landlocked nation on the continent, after [[Chad]]. Its predominantly Muslim population of about 29 million lives mostly in the south and west, and its capital, [[Niamey]], lies on the Niger River. After the spread of [[Islam]] to the region, the territory lay on the fringes of states including the [[Kanem–Bornu Empire]] and the [[Mali Empire]], and later became part of the [[Songhai Empire]]. France colonized it as part of French West Africa, making it a distinct colony in 1922. Since independence in 1960 it has experienced five coups and four periods of military rule. Following a 2023 coup it has been ruled by a military junta led by President Abdourahamane Tiani. The Hausa are the largest ethnic group, at around 56% of the population. The economy relies on subsistence agriculture and exports of [[Uranium|uranium]] ore.

Armed conflict between [[Nigeria]] and the secessionist Republic of Biafra, which declared independence in 1967. Fought from July 1967 to January 1970, it followed anti-[[Igbo people|Igbo]] pogroms in the Northern Region in 1966. Nigerian forces captured coastal oil facilities and [[Port Harcourt]] and encircled Biafra, led by Lieutenant Colonel Chukwuemeka "Emeka" Odumegwu Ojukwu. A blockade led to mass starvation. Around 100,000 military casualties occurred, while between 500,000 and 2 million Biafran civilians died of starvation. Images of starving children made it one of the first wars televised to a global audience. The [[United Kingdom]] and the [[Soviet Union]] backed the Nigerian government, while [[France]], [[Ivory Coast]] and [[Gabon]] supported Biafra. The war also led to the political marginalization of the Igbo people, as Nigeria has had no Igbo president since, a fact some observers cite as evidence of oppression.

Period of darkness when the [[Sun]] is below the [[Horizon|horizon]], the opposite of daytime. Earth's rotation causes sunrise and sunset, and moonlight, airglow, starlight and light pollution dimly illuminate the night. Its duration varies with the time of year and the observer's latitude. Night lasts about 58 Earth days on [[Venus]], and nights on [[Mercury (planet)|Mercury]] are also much longer than on Earth. Organisms respond to darkness, lower temperatures and higher humidity, and their behavior is governed in part by [[Circadian rhythm|circadian rhythms]]. Plants store energy from [[Photosynthesis|photosynthesis]] as starch to use at night, and many desert plants gather [[Carbon dioxide|carbon dioxide]] overnight for daytime photosynthesis. Light pollution is especially harmful to night-flying insects. Historically, night was a time of increased danger, and the fear of the dark remains common, especially among children. Artificial lighting has extended daytime activities into the night.

1968 American [[Zombie|zombie]] horror film directed by George A. Romero, who co-wrote it with John Russo. Its ensemble cast, led by Duane Jones, plays people trapped in a farmhouse in rural [[Pennsylvania]] by flesh-eating reanimated corpses. Shot on a budget of about US$100,000, it premiered in [[Pittsburgh]] in October 1968. It grossed US$12 million domestically and earned more than 250 times its budget. Because it was released without a copyright notice, it entered the [[Public domain|public domain]], enabling many adaptations. The [[Library of Congress]] selected it for the National Film Registry in 1999.

Purge in [[Nazi Germany]] carried out from 30 June to 2 July 1934, ordered by [[Adolf Hitler]] and urged on by [[Hermann Göring]] and [[Heinrich Himmler]]. It targeted leaders of the Sturmabteilung (SA), including chief of staff Ernst Röhm, whose plan to merge the SA with the army alarmed the military. The [[Schutzstaffel|Schutzstaffel]] (SS) and [[Gestapo]] under [[Reinhard Heydrich]] carried out most killings. Victims also included conservative critics such as former chancellor Kurt von Schleicher. At least 85 people died, though estimates run from 700 to 1,000, and more than 1,000 opponents were arrested.

Family (Caprimulgidae) of medium-sized nocturnal or crepuscular [[Bird|birds]] in the order Caprimulgiformes, characterized by long wings, short legs and very short bills. Some [[New World|New World]] species are called nighthawks. Nightjars occur on every continent except Antarctica, and on island groups such as the Seychelles and New Caledonia. They usually nest on the ground and often rest on roads. Their cryptic plumage and unusual perching habits help conceal them during the day, although many have contrasting pale patches or spots. The common poorwill undergoes a form of hibernation, becoming torpid with a much reduced body temperature for weeks or months. Traditionally the family was divided into two subfamilies, but molecular studies show that they are not monophyletic. The closest known relatives of nightjars are the extinct Archaeotrogonidae, known from the [[Eocene|Eocene]] and Oligocene of Europe.

[[Clothing|Clothing]] designed to be worn while sleeping, also called sleepwear or nightclothes. Styles vary with the seasons, with warmer ones worn in colder conditions. Variants include nightgowns, usually made of [[Cotton|cotton]], [[Silk|silk]], satin or [[Nylon|nylon]]; nightshirts; traditionally loose, two-piece pajamas; negligees of sheer fabric trimmed with lace; and adult onesies. Other garments commonly worn for sleep include gym shorts, T-shirts and [[Underwear|underwear]], and sleeping nude is common in warmer climates. A 2004 United States survey found that 13% of men wear pajamas or nightgowns for sleeping, compared with 31% who wear underwear and 31% who sleep nude. In the United States, children's sleepwear sized 0 to 14 is regulated under the Flammable Fabrics Act.

Finnish symphonic metal band formed in 1996 in Kitee by keyboardist Tuomas Holopainen, guitarist Emppu Vuorinen and vocalist Tarja Turunen. Albums including *Oceanborn* (1998), *Wishmaster* (2000) and *Once* (2004) brought international recognition. Turunen was dismissed in 2005, and Floor Jansen became lead vocalist in 2013, leaving the band in October 2026. The band has sold more than 10 million records and is the third-best-selling musical act in Finland, with nearly 900,000 certified sales. It was inducted into the Finnish Music Hall of Fame in 2018.

Family of philosophical views that reject the existence of any objectively meaningful purpose, moral value, truth or knowledge. Existential nihilism holds that life has no objective meaning or purpose, and moral nihilism denies the objective existence of morality. In [[Epistemology|epistemology]], nihilism challenges knowledge and truth; [[Relativism|relativism]] holds that they are relative to individuals or cultures, while skeptical views deny that they exist. In [[Metaphysics|metaphysics]], one form holds that the universe could have been empty of any objects. The idea emerged in the 18th and 19th centuries, particularly in Germany and Russia, through the works of Friedrich Heinrich Jacobi and [[Ivan Turgenev|Ivan Turgenev]]. [[Friedrich Nietzsche|Friedrich Nietzsche]] saw it as a cultural trend in which people lose traditional values as a result of secularization. In the 20th century, nihilist themes appeared in [[Dada|Dadaism]], [[Existentialism|existentialism]] and postmodern philosophy.

American athletic footwear and apparel corporation headquartered near Beaverton, Oregon. It is the world's largest supplier of athletic shoes and apparel and a major manufacturer of [[Sports equipment|sports equipment]]. Founded in 1964 as Blue Ribbon Sports by [[Phil Knight]] and Bill Bowerman, it officially became Nike, Inc. in 1971, named after the Greek goddess of victory. Its brands include Air Jordan and the Converse subsidiary, and its slogan "Just Do It" and Swoosh logo are widely recognized. Revenue was in excess of US$46 billion in fiscal 2022, and the company employed 83,700 people in 2024.

Austrian racing driver, motorsport executive and [[Aviation|aviation]] entrepreneur. He competed in [[Formula One|Formula One]] from 1971 to 1979 and from 1982 to 1985, winning three World Drivers' Championship titles. He is the only driver to have won a title with both Ferrari and [[McLaren|McLaren]]. He was seriously injured in a 1976 crash at the German Grand Prix, suffering severe burns, and returned to racing six weeks later. He founded airlines including Lauda Air and Niki. From 2012 he was non-executive chairman and co-owner of Mercedes, whose team won six consecutive World Constructors' Championships from 2014 to 2019.

Soviet politician who was First Secretary of the [[Communist Party of the Soviet Union|Communist Party]] from 1953 to 1964 and chairman of the Council of Ministers from 1958 to 1964. He denounced his predecessor [[Joseph Stalin]] in a 1956 "Secret Speech" at the 20th Party Congress, launching de-Stalinization. During Stalin's rule he had actively supported the [[Great Purge]]. After Stalin's death in 1953 he eliminated his rival [[Lavrentiy Beria]] and consolidated power. His domestic policies, especially in agriculture, were often ineffective, though his anti-religious campaign was more successful. He ordered major cuts in conventional forces and presided over the [[Cuban Missile Crisis]] in 1962. His popularity in the late 1950s rested partly on the launch of Sputnik in 1957. He was ousted in October 1964 and wrote memoirs, published in part in 1970.

Serbian [[Basketball|basketball]] player and center for the Denver Nuggets of the [[National Basketball Association]]. He is an eight-time NBA All-Star and a three-time NBA Most Valuable Player. He led the Nuggets to their first NBA championship in 2023 and was named Finals MVP. Selected 41st overall in the 2014 draft, he is the lowest-drafted player to win either the MVP or Finals MVP award. He has also played for Serbia, winning a silver medal at the 2016 Summer Olympics and a bronze at the 2024 Summer Olympics.

Serbian-American engineer, futurist and inventor known for his contributions to the design of the modern [[Alternating current|alternating current]] (AC) electricity supply system. Born in the Austro-Hungarian Empire, he emigrated to the United States in 1884 and became a naturalized citizen. After brief work at the [[Thomas Edison|Edison]] Machine Works in New York City, he set up his own laboratories and companies. His AC induction motor and polyphase patents, licensed to [[George Westinghouse|Westinghouse]] Electric in 1888, became the cornerstone of the polyphase system the company marketed. His unfinished Wardenclyffe Tower project, intended for wireless power transmission, ran out of funding. He spent his last years in New York hotels, leaving unpaid bills. In 1960 the General Conference on Weights and Measures named the magnetic flux density unit in the [[International System of Units]] the [[Tesla (unit)|tesla]] in his honor. In 2013, *Time* magazine named him one of the 100 most significant figures of all time.

Russian revolutionary, Soviet politician and Marxist theorist. Described by [[Vladimir Lenin]] as a "most valuable and major theorist" of the Communist Party, he became editor of *Pravda* after the [[October Revolution]]. In 1921 he became the chief theorist of the New Economic Policy, and by late 1924 he was [[Joseph Stalin|Stalin]]'s chief ally. Labelled the leader of the Right Opposition, he was removed from party leadership in 1929. He later edited *Izvestia* and was a principal architect of the 1936 Soviet Constitution. Accused of treason during the [[Great Purge]], he was later executed after a show trial.

Russian novelist, short-story writer and playwright of Ukrainian origin. He used the grotesque in stories such as "The Nose", "Viy", "The Overcoat" and "Nevsky Prospekt", which have been noted for their proto-surrealist qualities. His early works, such as *Evenings on a Farm Near Dikanka*, drew on Ukrainian folklore, while later works satirized political corruption, including *The Government Inspector* and *Dead Souls*. He enjoyed the patronage of Tsar Nicholas I. His influence was acknowledged by [[Fyodor Dostoevsky]], [[Franz Kafka]], [[Mikhail Bulgakov]], [[Vladimir Nabokov]] and others. Eugène-Melchior de Vogüé said: "We all came out from under Gogol's Overcoat."

Russian mathematician and geometer known for developing [[Non-Euclidean geometry|non-Euclidean geometry]], also called hyperbolic or Lobachevskian geometry, independently of János Bolyai. He replaced the parallel postulate of [[Euclid]] with the statement that through a point not on a given line more than one line can be drawn parallel to it. In hyperbolic geometry the angles of a triangle sum to less than 180 degrees. He first presented the idea in 1826, and his papers appeared in [[Kazan]] from 1829 to 1830. William Kingdon Clifford called him the "Copernicus of Geometry". He was rector of Kazan University from 1827 until 1846. Non-Euclidean geometry stimulated the development of [[Differential geometry|differential geometry]], which has many applications.
